issues.legal_issue: A tenant's unlawful subletting at the time notice terminating the tenancy is served gives rise to liability for eviction even if the subletting ends before the eviction suit is filed.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit alleging that the tenant had unlawfully sublet two rooms.
The courts found that the unlawful subletting existed when the landlord served notice terminating the tenancy.
The subtenant vacated after the notice was served but before the eviction suit was filed.
The lower courts granted eviction, and the Supreme Court dismissed the tenant's appeal.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was liable to eviction because unlawful subletting was proved to exist when the notice terminating the tenancy was served; it did not have to continue until the suit was filed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, proof that the tenant has unlawfully sublet makes the tenant liable to eviction. The Court adopted the interpretation in Maganlal Narandas Thakkar v. Arjan Bhanji Kanbi. It distinguished Goppulal v. Thakurji Shriji Dwarkadheeshji, which concerned subletting before rent-control legislation applied and did not decide whether subletting had to continue on the date of suit.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_for_unlawful_suble: A landlord brought a rent-control eviction proceeding alleging that the tenant unlawfully sublet the premises.
predicates.unlawful_subletting_at_notice: The landlord proved that the tenant's unlawful subletting existed when notice terminating the tenancy was served.

issues.definition: When a landlord brings a rent-control eviction proceeding for unlawful subletting and proves that the subletting existed when termination notice was served, the tenant is liable to eviction.
